title: Volume 6 · Payroll and Malaysian Statutory Deductions
subtitle: Lessons 1–10: salary structures, the monthly run, EPF, SOCSO, EIS and PCB, the salary journal and the remittances
outcomes: Build a salary structure whose components map one to one onto the payslip
Run a monthly payroll, verify one slip by hand, and explain every deduction on it
Post the salary journal so wages, statutory liabilities and net pay each land correctly
Remit the statutory amounts, prove the accounts clear, and close payroll month end

slides.title: Five outputs, one of which is not a document
bullets: A payslip per employee, a payroll register, a salary journal, statutory remittances, and the annual earnings statement
The slip is the employee's evidence, so every line must be explainable in a sentence
The journal is the accountant's evidence, and it must reconcile to the register to the cent
Statutory remittances are the compliance evidence, and the deadline is the risk, not the calculation
None of the five is a spreadsheet, and all five must exist before you call payroll live
slides.notes: Say the five outputs out loud at the start of the payroll workshop. Clients ask for the payslip and forget the journal; accountants ask for the journal and forget the annual statement. Naming all five at once sets the acceptance criteria for the whole build.

slides.title: Components, structure and the assignment
bullets: A salary component is one line on a payslip: basic, allowance, overtime, EPF, SOCSO, EIS, PCB, loan recovery
Components are typed as earnings or deductions, and the type decides the arithmetic on the slip
A salary structure groups the components into the shape of one month's pay
The structure is assigned to an employee with an effective date, which is how a raise is recorded rather than retyped
Keep the component list short and named the way the payslip should read

rows: Create the allowances the client actually pays
Build the structure from those components
Assign the structure to the employee
Open the slip preview for one month

slides.notes: The test of a component list is whether an employee could read their payslip without asking a question. If a line says 'miscellaneous allowance', it will be queried every month until somebody renames it.

slides.title: Four deductions, four liabilities, four deadlines
bullets: EPF is a retirement contribution with an employee share and an employer share, both computed on wage bands
SOCSO covers employment injury and invalidity, and the employer share is larger than the employee share
EIS is employment insurance, small, and easy to forget because it rarely moves the net pay much
PCB is monthly tax deduction, calculated from annualised income, reliefs and rebates rather than a flat percentage
Rates and wage ceilings are schedule values that change, so confirm the current ones with the client's payroll advisor

rows: Figure derived from the tax setup
Each deduction has its own account

slides.notes: Do not memorise percentages; memorise the structure. Employee share, employer share, wage ceiling, and a tax figure that is calculated. Rates change and a consultant who quotes last year's number in a workshop loses the room, so the discipline is to confirm the schedule and record who confirmed it.

slides.title: Making PCB a calculation rather than an opinion
bullets: The income tax slab holds the progressive rates, the reliefs and the rebates the calculation uses
Verify the slab against the current published schedule before the first payroll run, and date the check
Personal reliefs and rebates materially change a low-wage slip, so they belong in the setup rather than a note
An employee's tax number belongs on the record; without it the annual statement is incomplete
A manual PCB override is allowed, but it must be documented or it becomes an untraceable habit

rows: Enter the current brackets from the published schedule
Attach the slab to the payroll run
A computed figure, not a blank
Record the schedule date and source
Dated note in the payroll file

slides.notes: The slab is where a consultant is closest to giving tax advice, so stay on the right side of the line: configure what the published schedule says, date the check, and let the advisor confirm the treatment of anything unusual.

slides.title: One payroll entry, reviewed one slip at a time
bullets: Payroll Entry is the monthly driver: it selects the employees and creates their slips in one action
Run it for the period, then read one slip line by line before submitting anything
A slip that looks wrong is usually a missing assignment or a stale structure, not a calculation bug
Submit the run only after the register totals agree with your own expected total
Keep a copy of the register with the run, because it is the evidence that the month was checked

rows: Create a payroll entry for the period
Open one slip and read every line
Compare the register total to your expectation

slides.notes: Read one slip completely rather than scrolling ten. A consultant who can explain a single payslip line by line will catch a misassigned structure immediately, whereas a scan of the register hides it in a total that looks plausible.

slides.title: Do the arithmetic by hand, once per month
bullets: Take one employee and compute gross, each statutory deduction and net pay on paper
The employer shares are a cost, not a deduction, so they never reduce net pay and always increase the journal
A difference of a few sen is rounding; a difference of a few ringgit is a band, a ceiling or a wrong structure
Check the slip against the register, then check the register against your own total
Sign the check, because a payroll that nobody verified is a guess with a document attached

rows: EPF, SOCSO, EIS, PCB per schedule
Cost on top of gross, not deducted

slides.notes: Use a worked example in the lab, on a gross of three thousand, and compute it by hand: employee EPF, SOCSO, EIS, the tax figure the slab produces, then net. The exercise exists to build the habit, because a consultant who cannot verify a slip cannot defend one.

slides.title: Where the money actually goes
bullets: Gross wages are an expense, split by cost centre when the client wants labour cost per department
Employee deductions are liabilities owed to EPF, SOCSO, EIS and the tax authority, not reductions in expense
Employer contributions are additional expense with their own liabilities, which is why the journal is larger than net pay
Net pay becomes a payable to employees until the bank transfer clears it
The journal must balance against the register, and the proof is the total of the four liabilities

rows: Open the journal created by the payroll run
Check wages hit the salary expense account
Check net pay sits as a payable
Post the journal and read the ledger

slides.notes: The journal is where a functional consultant proves they understand payroll: wages are expense, deductions are liabilities, employer shares are extra cost. Show the four liabilities as four accounts, because lumping them into one payable makes the monthly remittance a reconciliation exercise.

slides.title: The deadline is the compliance event
bullets: Each statutory body has its own payment and filing date, and they are not all the same day
Pay the authority from the liability account so the account clears to zero by the deadline
Keep the receipt or acknowledgement with the payroll month, not in an inbox
The annual earnings statement is produced from the same records, so a clean month makes a clean year
A late remittance is a penalty regardless of whether the calculation was perfect
slides.notes: Clients remember the deduction and forget the remittance date, so put the dates in the client's calendar with an owner, not in the handover document. A liability that never clears is either an unpaid remittance or a double payment, and both are found by looking at the account.

slides.title: The messy months, handled in order
bullets: A leaver needs a final slip with prorated wages, leave encashment and cleared advances, before the record is closed
Proration uses the joining or leaving date, so the first and last months are the ones that go wrong
Arrears from a late raise are a separate adjustment, documented with the reason and the period
Never edit a submitted slip; reverse and re-run, because the trail is the defence
Close the employee record with a date, so headcount and statutory reports stay honest

rows: Set the relieving date on the employee
Proration applied to the final slip
Line appears on the final slip
Pay a late raise as a documented arrears line
Reverse a wrong slip rather than editing it

slides.notes: The leaver's month is where the employee is most attentive and least forgiving, so do it in order: prorate, encash, clear advances, then pay. And never edit a submitted slip — a reversal with a reason is defensible, an edit is not.

slides.title: Four checks that close payroll
bullets: The register total equals the journal total, and both equal your hand calculation
Every statutory liability cleared to zero by the remittance, or explained with a date
Salary payable to employees is zero after the bank transfer, with no lingering advances
Headcount on the register equals headcount on the employee list, leavers included
File the month: register, journal, four acknowledgements and the signed verification
slides.notes: Four checks, ten minutes, once a month, and payroll stops being frightening. The file matters as much as the checks: a month with no acknowledgements stored is a month you cannot prove was remitted, whatever the ledger says.

lab.title: Lab · Run one payroll month for Seri Murni and prove it
steps: Build the salary components and one structure for a gross of 3,000.00 with transport of 200.00
Create the four statutory deduction components and assign each its own liability account
Enter the current income tax slab from the published schedule and date the source you used
Assign the structure to the employee from 2026-03-01 and preview one month's slip
Run the payroll entry for March, open one slip and read every line before submitting
Compute gross, employee EPF, SOCSO, EIS, the tax figure and net pay by hand, then compare
Post the salary journal and confirm wages, employer shares, four liabilities and net payable
Remit the four amounts, prove the accounts clear to zero, and file the month with its acknowledgements
lab.done: One month of payroll that reconciles three ways — hand calculation, salary slip and journal — with four statutory liabilities cleared to zero and a dated payroll file holding the register, journal and acknowledgements.

quiz.question: Which of payroll's five outputs is not a document for an individual?
options: The payslip
The salary journal, which is the accounting evidence for the whole run
The annual statement
The remittance receipt
quiz.why: The other four relate to a person or an authority. The journal is the aggregate that must equal the register, and it is the output clients forget to define acceptance criteria for.

quiz.question: How should employer EPF, SOCSO and EIS shares be treated?
options: As deductions from gross pay
As additional expense with their own liabilities, on top of gross
As part of net pay
As a reduction in the salary expense account
quiz.why: The employee share reduces net pay; the employer share is extra cost. That is why the journal is larger than net pay and why lumping them into one payable hides the employer cost.

quiz.question: What does a difference of a few ringgit between your hand calculation and the slip most likely indicate?
options: Rounding
A wrong wage band, an ignored ceiling or a stale structure assignment
A missing bank account
A tax rate that changed mid-year
quiz.why: Sen are rounding; ringgit are structural. Check the band, the ceiling and whether the employee still carries an old structure before looking for a calculation fault.

quiz.question: Why must statutory liabilities sit in four separate accounts?
options: Because the chart of accounts requires it
Because each authority is paid separately, and the account must clear to zero
Because PCB is not a liability
Because employer shares are not liabilities
quiz.why: Separate accounts make the monthly remittance a lookup rather than a reconciliation. One lumped payable cannot tell you which authority is unpaid.

quiz.question: What is the correct way to fix a submitted salary slip that is wrong?
options: Edit the slip and resubmit
Reverse it and create a corrected slip with the reason recorded
Delete it and run payroll again
Adjust the next month's slip silently
quiz.why: A reversal plus a new slip leaves a trail. Editing or deleting destroys the evidence that payroll was ever wrong, which is exactly what an auditor or a disputed payslip needs.

memory.spine: Gross is expense, deductions are liabilities, employer shares are cost, and every liability must clear to zero by its deadline.

device.label: Gross, statutory, net, remit
expansion: Gross wages are expense, split by cost centre where labour cost is measured
Employee deductions are four liabilities owed to four authorities, never a reduction in expense
Employer shares are extra cost on top of gross, with their own liabilities
Net pay is a payable to employees until the bank transfer clears it
Every liability clears to zero at remittance, and the month is filed with acknowledgements

cards.q: What are the five outputs a payroll month must produce?
cards.a: Payslips, a payroll register, the salary journal, the statutory remittances, and data sufficient for the annual earnings statement.

cards.q: Why is the journal larger than net pay?
cards.a: Because gross includes employer EPF, SOCSO and EIS shares as extra expense, while net pay is gross minus the employee's deductions only.

cards.q: What belongs in the income tax setup, and what must be dated?
cards.a: The published brackets, reliefs and rebates from the current schedule — and a dated note of the source and who confirmed it.

cards.q: What proves a payroll month is finished?
cards.a: Register equals journal, four statutory liabilities at zero after remittance, salary payable cleared, headcount agreed, and the month filed.

cards.q: How is a leaver's final month assembled?
cards.a: Prorate from the relieving date, encash remaining leave, clear advances, then pay — and close the employee record with a date.

trap.what: The first payroll runs, the payslips look right, and nobody checks the journal — so the statutory liabilities sit in one account and go unpaid until a penalty arrives.
trap.why: A correct slip is not a correct month. Four separate liability accounts, a remittance calendar with owners, and four month-end checks make the compliance visible before an authority asks.

narration: Payroll is five outputs, not one: a payslip per person, a register, a salary journal, four statutory remittances, and enough data to produce the annual statement. Build it from components and a structure, assigned with an effective date, so a raise is a new assignment rather than a retyped slip. Then treat the statutory side structurally rather than from memory: a four layer deduction with an employee share, an employer share, a wage ceiling and a tax figure that is calculated from a slab. Rates change, so confirm the current schedule with the client's payroll advisor and date the check. Run the month through the payroll entry, but read one slip line by line and compute it by hand once, because a consultant who cannot verify a payslip cannot defend one. The journal is where understanding shows: gross wages are expense, deductions are liabilities to four authorities, employer shares are extra cost, and net pay is a payable until the bank clears it. Then remit, prove the four accounts clear to zero, and file the month with its acknowledgements. Leavers get prorated, encashed and cleared in that order, and a wrong slip is reversed, never edited.
